items.title: This implant can restore sight for patients with macular degeneration
items.raw_text: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) affects more than 5 million people around the world. And until now, no treatment could restore their vision. The Prima system, which was approved in Europe in July and is awaiting FDA clearance in the US, changes that. It combines a retinal implant with camera-­equipped eyeglasses to improve sight in patients who develop a blind spot in the middle of their vision due to advanced AMD. After training sessions, more than 80% of recipients were able to read, do crosswords, and use their phones. The retina processes light in three layers of cells: Photoreceptors convert light into electricity, bipolar cells process that signal, and ganglion cells transmit the signal to the optic nerve and the brain. Prima replaces the photoreceptors. BROWN BIRD DESIGN Developed by the California-based Science Corporation, the system takes advantage of the fact that AMD doesn’t damage all retinal circuitry; only photoreceptors—the cells that convert light into an electrical signal—die off. Prima’s implant mimics those cells and transmits visual information directly to healthy eye circuitry and on to the brain. “We’re leveraging all of the body’s own natural functions to process and transmit the information,” says Frank Brodie, an ophthalmologist at the University of California, San Francisco, and medical director for Prima. I can conjure the sensation of stroking her while she purred, recall how she used to get stuck in trees (just like in cartoons!), and chuckle about the time she pooed in my baby sister’s cot. That’s about it. What I do vividly remember, though, is the day she went missing. I was 10 years old, and I searched everywhere for her, scouting nearby fields and woods until sunset. I made posters. We never found her. I was devastated. There was no way to get more time with Peppy, but almost 30 years later, pet owners are being offered an ever-expanding set of options to potentially prolong their years with their furry companions. The possibilities include drugs, cloning, and even cryonics. But is that a good thing? There’s certainly a market for pet preservation. items.title: Kids are outsmarting social media bans. That’s not a problem we need to solve.
items.raw_text: Social media bans are stacking up. In July, France joined Australia in restricting minors from accessing social media—barring children under 15 from major platforms, before the ban was blocked by the country’s top court on human rights grounds. The UK aims to forbid kids under 16 from accessing Facebook, TikTok, and other platforms in early 2027, and the EU has announced its own plan to prohibit social media for kids under 15. But early lessons from Australia, which enacted a ban in 2024, show that these sorts of age restrictions are easily circumvented. A study published earlier this year found that four in five teens under 16 made their way onto barred platforms. Teens have successfully explored many tactics for bypassing bans, from using a sibling’s face for ID to drawing fake facial hair. Some proponents of bans have called for an increased focus on enforcement that blocks these workarounds. But circumvention is a signal, not a nuisance or something to be simply deterred. The fact that kids are actively looking for ways to outwit the bans highlights their limitations. Social media bans suppress kids’ access to information, including information that’s essential to their development, identity formation, and socialization, especially during adolescence. Worse, further restriction is likely to backfire. Closing loopholes in age gates could harm kids by pushing them toward less-moderated, higher-risk corners of the web. items.title: OpenAlex Announces Launch of Trusted Journal Lists
items.raw_text: From an OpenAlex Post: Trust in science is under more pressure than it has been in a long time. Paper mills, hijacked journals, citation rings and a flood of machine-written manuscripts mean that “is this a real journal?” is now a question every reader, reviewer, funder and university has to ask. And the tools for answering it have not kept up. The traditional answer is a deny list. Something like the old Beall’s List : a roster of predatory journals, so you can filter them out of a search, an evaluation, a systematic review. We understand the appeal. Nobody wants to cite a paper mill by accident. But we’re not building a deny list, and we don’t think you want one either. Librarians have been making this case for a decade : deny lists are opaque , they go stale the moment they’re published, they’re a lawsuit magnet , and they land hardest on exactly the journals that can least absorb the hit… small, new, non-English, Global South. Beall’s List went dark in 2017 . The advice since then has been consistent: don’t filter out the bad, filter in the good. Use allow lists . items.title: How much more can nuclear power plants give?
items.raw_text: In this age of rising electricity demand, people are trying to squeeze every last bit of power out of every power plant possible. Over the past few weeks, there’s been big news about nuclear power plants trying to do just that. Constellation, the largest nuclear operator in the US, announced plans to add nearly a gigawatt of new capacity across 11 existing nuclear reactors at six plants. And on October 5, the Department of Energy awarded a $4.2 billion loan to Vistra for previously announced upgrades at three plants. Pushing existing reactors to produce more could help provide more clean power for data centers, quickly. But just how much additional power can we count on? Upgrading equipment at existing nuclear power plants can allow them to reach a higher capacity; the process is called a power uprate. Operators have been doing this since the 1970s in the US, but it’s been less common in recent years as demand for electricity plateaued and cheap natural gas put financial pressure on nuclear power plants. Some plants closed, and putting in more money to produce more electricity didn’t make much sense at others. Between 2001 and 2010, the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission approved over 80 uprates. Between 2011 and 2020, the number was 33. But with the rise of AI and the related boom in electricity demand, there’s been a shift. KDE turns 30 with Plasma 6.8, remote upgrades, and an X11 farewell
items.raw_text: Marking the 30th anniversary of software developer KDE on October 14, the company released Plasma 6.8, debuted a movie, and retired Plasma's native X11 session support. The announcement from KDE dubs the new Plasma 6.8 as the "30th Anniversary Edition" and describes the update as preparing Plasma for the future. Legacy X11 applications will still function via the XWayland compatibility layer , and KDE applications will also continue supporting X11 under other desktop environments. After 42 years in service, the X11 protocol is losing another major desktop environment. Plasma will fully adopt the Wayland system and put support for starting new X11 sessions in Plasma to bed. Users opting to stay on Plasma 6.7 will keep their existing sessions for now. The move was expected, with GNOME officially dropping X11 sessions by default in 2025 . The new Plasma 6.8 brings many improvements, including increased support for adding window decorations (like shadows and rounded corners) to third-party apps, and a more streamlined Union theming system . Other notable additions include Nvidia triple buffering being enabled by default, Kup backup integration (KDE's backup utility—now integrated into Plasma), and kscreenctl , a command-line utility that allows power users to adjust display configurations. items.raw_text: Plex, which made a name for itself by letting users share movies they own, is now helping sell movie theater tickets. The company is looking to monetize its content-discovery capabilities and expand its business beyond its media server software. Plex partnered with Fandango, which has sold movie tickets since 2000, to drive ticket sales from people searching for movies to stream. Per the announcement: Starting today, Plex users in the US will see a Fandango ticketing option on title pages for movies currently playing in theaters, allowing them to click through to Fandango to find showtimes and purchase tickets. The integration also enables direct attribution through Kochava, giving studios and advertisers greater visibility into how campaigns and audience engagement translate into ticket sales. Fandango says it sells tickets for 31,000 movie theater screens in the US. The Plex deal allows it to leverage data from Plex’s streaming service (Plex claims users of the service “make more than 100 million streaming decisions each month”), including "ratings and cross-platform viewing" to gain “insight into audience intent," the announcement said. items.title: Hegseth’s dubious low-T screening may flag up to 25 percent of the Army
items.raw_text: Up to a quarter of active-duty Army members could receive a low testosterone result from mandatory military screening, despite the true prevalence of the condition likely being a tiny fraction of that figure, according to a study published Thursday in JAMA . The finding adds to concerns that the mandatory screening announced by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in July will lead to a cascade of unnecessary medical evaluations for military members. Those evaluations could result in inappropriate testing, inaccurate results and diagnoses, and overtreatment that could cause harm, including infertility. Medical experts, including the Endocrine Society and the American Urological Association (AUA), have recommended against blanket screenings for these reasons. Still, the Pentagon has moved forward with the plans, releasing clinical guidance in September . The JAMA study highlights the reasons why testosterone levels are not measured in men without symptoms—and also offers a glimpse of how many Army members could become ensnared in the clinically dubious screenings. items.raw_text: Researchers say that mercenary hackers laced ads with zero-click exploits that installed sophisticated malware on the devices of targeted individuals when they did nothing other than load a website or open an installed app. The finding, published Thursday by the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab, said the incident is likely to be the first confirmation of zero-click mercenary spyware delivered through targeted ads. The attacks, which worked on iOS and Android devices, are particularly pernicious because they work without requiring any interaction from the target and are invisible unless users run special forensic hardware or software. Citizen Lab said it confirmed that AdFection, as it named the campaign, infected 45 devices at international media organization Al Jazeera in 2024 and 2025. A clear warning signal “This investigation should … serve as a clear warning signal to news organizations around the world that they may be being actively targeted via this new threat,” Citizen Lab researchers wrote. “This targeting may happen both in newsrooms and to individual journalists, editors, and other staff members.” Their report went on to say: “The distribution of spyware via targeted ads represents a security risk not only for potential victims but also for states and civil society at large.” Read full article Comments

items.title: What did the Liberty Bell sound like? Science is on the case.
items.raw_text: The Liberty Bell , with its famous crack, hasn't been rung in 180 years, but that hasn't stopped scientists from pondering what the bell might have sounded like when tolling. In honor of the nation's 250th anniversary, researchers at Penn State University have modeled its acoustic properties, drawing on data collected from one of the bell's replicas. The work was first presented at a meeting of the Acoustical Society of America in Philadelphia earlier this year, followed by an article in Physics Today. Historians aren't sure exactly when the Liberty Bell acquired its distinctive crack, just that it occurred sometime between 1817 and 1846. An 1846 account in the Public Ledger described the ringing of the bell on February 23 that year and mentioned that the bell had developed a crack, which someone had attempted to fix by filing the sides down. But it didn't work: The February 23 ringing extended the crack even more, so much so that "the old Independence Bell ... now hangs in the great steeple irreparably cracked and forever dumb." Nobody has heard it ring since. This wasn't the first time the bell had cracked; the rim cracked shortly after it arrived in Philadelphia in 1752, the first time the clapper struck while testing the sound. It was recast by two local foundry workers, John Pass and John Stow, not once but twice, because the first recast produced a sound that one bystander likened to coal scuttles banging together. items.title: Microplastics in water aren’t inert and make damaging chemicals on their own
items.raw_text: One reason plastics are used so often is that they’re chemically inert, meaning bags, food containers, and cups don't react with what we put in them. Yet they can still break down into microplastics, which turn up in drinking water, human blood, arteries, and brains. The consequences of that are uncertain. “Whether microplastics can directly cause human disease is still being researched,” said Wei Min, a chemist at Columbia University. In a new Nature study, Min's team took a step toward answering this question by demonstrating that microplastics are likely not as chemically inert as we might expect. Microdroplet chemistry Min's lab has spent years working on microdroplet chemistry, studying how water broken into tiny droplets behaves at its boundary with air. These droplets have been reported to generate reactive oxygen species, or ROS, a family of harmful, oxygen-containing molecules. “ROS will essentially bump into proteins, lipids, DNA, and cause damage,” Min said. “You could break a DNA strand into segments. You could mutate DNA; you could misfold proteins.” Read full article Comments

items.title: Neutron's first launch slips again amid trouble with carbon composites
items.raw_text: Rocket Lab announced Wednesday that its Neutron launch vehicle won't fly until 2027, citing an issue discovered during manufacturing of the rocket's carbon composite structures. The announcement was public confirmation of what nearly everyone inside Rocket Lab and the wider space industry already knew. The most recent official update from Rocket Lab in August suggested the company still held hope of delivering the first Neutron rocket to its launch pad at Wallops Island, Virginia, before the end of this year, a schedule that would have almost certainly pushed the first flight into 2027. But Rocket Lab's statement Wednesday about Neutron's schedule suggests the company is still struggling with manufacturing the rocket's large booster stage. Neutron's reusable first stage is made of carbon composite structures, which offer low weight, high strength, and corrosion resistance. items.title: Rewilding could help vulnerable islands keep pace with rising seas
items.raw_text: Coral-fringed tropical atolls are among the landforms most threatened by global warming, but many have a potential superpower: Healthy ecosystems may help them keep pace with rising seas. Atoll islands with native vegetation and thriving seabird populations are “naturally active systems that can change and adapt to their environmental conditions if they are allowed to do so,” said Nick Graham , a marine ecologist at Lancaster University in the United Kingdom, who led an international team of scientists that studied island resilience across 28 atoll islands in the Pacific and Indian oceans. Their paper, published Wednesday in Science Advances , shows that restoring atoll ecosystems reinforces their growth. Seabirds ferry nutrients from the open ocean and deposit them on the atolls as guano that nurtures land plants, marine life and coral growth. This provides more material for reef building, as parrotfish and other reef feeders turn dead coral into sand to maintain beaches, while native plants with extensive root networks stabilize sediments. items.raw_text: Begin deze maand is China’s herziene Nationale Defensie Mobilisatie-wet van kracht geworden. Het Europees Parlement (EP) nam in Straatsburg unaniem een motie van Bart Groothuis (VVD) aan, die deze wet scherp veroordeelt. Het Chinese leger krijgt bij een mobilisatie direct de macht over alle data, technologie en software van Chinese bedrijven. Volgens europarlementariër Bart Groothuis (VVD) horen Chinese bedrijven daarom niet thuis in onze kritieke infrastructuur. Volgens de liberale europarlementariër strekt de greep van het Chinese leger zich nu uit tot Europese dochters van Chinese bedrijven. Onder de nieuwe bepalingen vallen ook buitenlandse en binnenlandse bedrijven onder het bereik van de wet. Dringende noodzaak Groothuis: ‘De nieuwe wet benadrukt dat bedrijven die onder deze wet vallen geen betrouwbare leveranciers kunnen zijn voor de kritieke infrastructuur van Europa. Het onderstreept ook de dringende noodzaak om de kritieke ict-toeleveringsketens minder risicovol te maken.’ Het Europees Parlement (EP) schaart zich unaniem achter zijn motie die deze wet scherp veroordeelt. De hele Chinese techsector, waaronder cybersecurity, ai , geavanceerde tech-applicaties en netwerk-veiligheid, gaat onder de herziene wet vallen. Hetzelfde geldt voor aanbieders van infrastructuur en logistiek. De wet is ruim geformuleerd en hanteert vage criteria voor toepassing wat het bereik vergroot. Overigens kent de VS ook dit soort wetgeving met extraterritoriale werking.

items.raw_text: Aanbieders van generatieve ai-diensten moeten zorgvuldiger omgaan met informatie over vergunningen en online-goksites. Daarvoor waarschuwt het Nederlandse Keurmerk Verantwoorde Affiliates (KVA). Na eigen onderzoek blijkt dat populaire ai‑systemen zoals ChatGPT Nederlandse consumenten foutief doorverwijzen naar illegale goksites. Die waarschuwing komt op het moment dat in de Verenigde Staten acht staten rechtszaken zijn gestart tegen OpenAI vanwege vermeende veiligheidsrisico’s van ChatGPT. Volgens KVA laat die internationale aandacht zien dat ook in Nederland sprake is van een groeiend probleem: Ai‑systemen geven onjuiste of misleidende antwoorden, bijvoorbeeld over de juridische status van online casino’s. Uit het onderzoek van KVA blijkt dat tien geteste ai‑tools, waaronder ChatGPT, Google Gemini en Microsoft Copilot, aanbieders zonder Nederlandse vergunning noemen bij relatief eenvoudige vragen. Bij acht systemen gebeurde dat al na neutrale of licht sturende consumentenvragen. ChatGPT verwees in alle drie de onderzochte vragenreeksen naar niet‑vergunde aanbieders. Bij Google Gemini, Microsoft Copilot en Mistral Le Chat ging het nog verder: deze systemen presenteerden illegale aanbieders als legaal of eigenaar van een geldige Nederlandse vergunning van de Kansspelautoriteit (KSA), terwijl dat niet zo is. ‘Zorgwekkend’ KVA‑vertegenwoordiger Steven Vrolijk ziet in de Amerikaanse rechtszaken aanleiding om de Nederlandse onderzoeksresultaten extra onder de aandacht te brengen.

Dagelijks vragen klanten om meer systemen. De chipmachinefabrikant ziet veel orderinstroom voor 2028, maar er is ook grote belangstelling om nu al bestellingen te plaatsen voor 2029 en soms zelfs 2030. Om zo goed mogelijk aan de vraag te voldoen besloot ASML afgelopen zomer al de capaciteit in 2027 met 30 procent te verhogen. De ambitie is om in 2028 opnieuw een groei van 30 procent te realiseren.
